content:
Ongoing lawsuit alleging Apple and OpenAI misappropriated trade secrets has seen a new development: OpenAI today filed a motion before a federal judge seeking to dismiss the case. OpenAI stated that Apple's complaint was "filed without a thorough investigation" and accused Apple of taking "normal conduct" out of context.

Meanwhile, Apple is currently pushing hard for an injunction, with a court hearing scheduled for October 1. The entire case could take years to resolve.

In this motion to dismiss, OpenAI is attempting to have the entire case thrown out as early as possible. OpenAI pointed out that Apple failed to meet the legal standard, unable to prove that it possessed specific trade secrets, nor could it reasonably allege any wrongdoing.

OpenAI argued that the examples Apple cited regarding former employees discussing confidential information were mischaracterised. The content of the iMessage conversations referenced by OpenAI was also published on its website earlier this week.

OpenAI stated that these messages show that one of the individuals named in the original complaint, Chang Liu, was asked by an Apple employee to retrieve the data, not acting in OpenAI's interest. OpenAI pointed out that Apple "did not allege that Mr. Liu disclosed any documents to OpenAI, or used any documents in OpenAI's hardware work".

Similarly, the motion to dismiss also responds to Apple's claim that former Apple vice president Tang Tan retained a document describing Apple's offboarding procedures.

Apple alleged that the document was used by Tan to help him circumvent various security checks when recruiting Apple employees. However, OpenAI in today's motion offered an alternative interpretation: that Tan used this information to ensure that the new employees he hired strictly followed Apple's offboarding procedures, so as to prevent any impropriety.

Of course, all this legal language is to be expected. We still don't know whether OpenAI's arguments can meet the statutory threshold required to dismiss the complaint, but we're not surprised they're trying to have the complaint thrown out—that's what lawyers do.

At least for now, neither OpenAI nor Apple seems to have any intention of settling. The next important procedural milestone will be the injunction hearing on October 1.
